exhibitions.caption: Human figures ride stylized leopards around this painted wooden seat. Cleveland attributes it to a Babanki-style maker in the Cameroon Grassfields. Such chairs helped mark kingships and also circulated as royal gifts and works for local or European patrons. Authority is carried through supports, animal imagery and the act of sitting.

A city’s authority fits inside this ring. Its gold hoop bears the date 1532, while the museum records a replacement sapphire bought in 1590. Kraków’s arms are cut into the stone so the civic insignia could also serve as a seal. The object joins public office, precious material and an image made to leave an impression.

This silver reliquary gives a container for saints’ relics the shape of the Holy Sepulchre. Its small architectural body links sacred remains to a place associated with Christ’s burial. Historical accounts identify its contents differently; the building-shaped container gives devotion a visible form.

A pillar surrounded by flames marks the Buddha’s presence in this limestone panel from Nagarjunakonda. Attendants hold fly whisks beside it; above, celestial beings praise another miraculous pillar. Sacred presence is conveyed through radiance, symbols and acts of veneration rather than a standing human figure.

Wyspiański painted white lilies on the pale blue panels of this wooden casket. Dark framing separates the plant compositions while the flowers repeat across front, back and sides. Turn the box to follow how a flat painted motif changes the character of a solid wooden volume.

Raised ceramic forms turn an image into an uneven surface. Książek set the glazed panel in cement within a metal frame; the museum relates the series to urban architecture and church towers. Moving around the relief changes how its lines, shadows and colored glazes divide the composition.

A Maya ballplayer dives toward a rubber ball, his padded torso prepared for impact. The stepped walls probably mark a ball court. Move around the vessel to find the scene: a curved ceramic surface holds a selected instant of bodily movement. Cleveland records that this vessel was repaired after breaking into 34 pieces.

This detached sandstone head comes from a deva at Preah Khan in Angkor. Its five-tiered lotus tiara and modeled face preserve part of a larger figure connected with the Churning of the Ocean of Milk. The head can be examined in detail, while the figure’s body, companions and architectural setting require other evidence.

An ivory panel carved around 1000 sits inside a fourteenth-century jeweled setting. Scenes of the Wedding at Cana survive within a later book-shaped reliquary made to hold gospel leaves and saints’ relics. The object joins work from different periods; its present form should not be assigned wholly to the ivory carver or to one date.

These gilt-bronze pillars once supported a stupa at Tibet’s Densatil Monastery. Bodhisattvas faced visitors, while offering goddesses faced inward toward the monument. A Tibetan syllable marked each support’s place in the larger structure. Turning the surviving objects reveals both sides, but the tiered sacred monument that organized their original viewing is absent.

A Chinese guardian lion lies on its back, holding a ball that supports a cub. The ball is the ink container. The arrangement turns a protective animal image into an elaborate object for writing, with cloisonné and champlevé color carried across the metal surface. Look for how the adult and cub organize the vessel.

A bat perches on the sleeping poet Li Taibo’s shoulder, while a deer nestles behind him. Cleveland connects the bat with good fortune and the deer with longevity and prosperity. Carved into a small piece of amber, the animals give a human figure an auspicious setting. Turn the group to find how they fit around the poet and his wine jar.
